o: Index i is stable when the maximum of the prefix nums[0..i] minus the minimum of the suffix nums[i..n-1] is at most k. Intuition: i is the 'handoff point' where everything before is not too much larger than everything from i onward. Example 1: scores are 5, 5, 4, 1 — index 3 is the first with score <= 3. Example 2: every score is 2 > 1, so -1. Example 3: a single element has score 0 <= 0, so index 0. Precompute prefix maxima left to right and suffix minima right to left, then scan for the first stable index — O(n).
k: instability[i] = prefixMax[i] - suffixMin[i], where both arrays include index i.
One left-to-right pass for prefix max, one right-to-left pass for suffix min, then a linear scan for the first i with difference <= k.

a.n: Approach 1: Precomputed prefix max and suffix min
a.i: Build prefMax[i] = max(nums[0..i]) in one pass and sufMin[i] = min(nums[i..n-1]) in another; stability is then a direct subtraction, and we return the first index meeting the threshold.
s: Scan i = 0..n-1; return the first i with prefMax[i] - sufMin[i] <= k.
a.sp: O(n) for the two auxiliary arrays.

a.n: Approach 2: Suffix-min array with running prefix max (less memory)
a.i: Keep only the suffix-min array; maintain the prefix max on the fly during the final scan, halving memory while keeping the same logic.
s: Scan i left to right maintaining runMax = max(nums[0..i]).
Return the first i with runMax - sufMin[i] <= k, else -1.
a.sp: O(n) for the suffix-min array (the prefix max is a scalar).

w: Either version is ideal; Approach 2 shows the memory optimization interviewers like. Pitfalls: the suffix min must include index i itself (off-by-one), and differences can reach 2e9 so use 64-bit in C++/Java. Edge cases: n = 1 (always stable, score 0), k = 0 (requires the prefix max to equal the suffix min). Follow-up: count stable indices, or find the smallest index with instability exactly k.
